catalog_locator: Section 4.1.2 'Polysyllabic words', p. 42 (Dara-ang of No-Lae, Fang, Chiang Mai); the parallel statement in section 5.1.2 'Polysyllabic words', p. 74 (Da-ang of Kalaw, Shan State) and viewed.
catalog_quote: p. 42: "The first type of polysyllabic words is called sequisyllabic. As found in other Mon-Khmer languages, sequisyllabic words have a stressed main syllable, which is preceded by an unstressed and phonological reduced minor syllable (Matisoff, 1973). The minor syllable can either be presyllable CV, as in (2a-b), or presyllabic nasal, as in (2c-d). Note that in Dara-ang the major stressed syllable of sequisyllabic words can be preceded by two presyllables CVCV, as in (2e-f)." (2) a. /dɨgaw/ 'pounded rice' b. /ʔimaj/ 'male, husband' c. /m phăn/ 'five (5)' d. /ɲ căh/ 'comb' e. /ma ŋ giah/ 'porcupine' f. /madɨgliah/ 'crab' ... "The second type of polysyllabic words are compound words, which are made by combining two words." p. 74: "The first type of polysyllabic word in the Da-ang Palaung dialect of Kalaw city is a sequisyllabic word, which has a stressed main syllable that is preceded by an unstressed and phonological reduced minor syllable. The minor syllable can either be presyllable CV, as in (2a-b), or presyllabic nasal, as in (2c-d). Note that, as found in Dara-ang, a major stressed syllable of a sequisyllabic word in Da-ang can be preceded by two presyllables CVCV, as in (2e-f)."
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record and no existing statement for ruch1235, so this is the first prose statement of stress placement for the language. It matches the pattern implicit in the earlier reading's transcriptions (Buakaw 2014, 2009: stress marked on the major syllable) and Buakaw, Rattanapitak & Deepadung 2018 on Katiang Palaung ('presyllable is an unstressed syllable').
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are monosyllables, sesquisyllables (one or two unstressed, phonologically reduced minor syllables + one major syllable) or compounds. In a sesquisyllabic word the stress falls on the major syllable, which is always the last syllable; the presyllable(s) or presyllabic nasal preceding it are unstressed. The statement is made for both dialects studied (Dara-ang, No-Lae, Thailand; Da-ang, Kalaw, Myanmar). Nothing is said about stress in compounds (which are treated as sequences of two words) or about tone; vowel length is phonemic and is the thesis's main topic.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The thesis explicitly allows a major stressed syllable to be preceded by two presyllables (CVCV), so stress is not simply 'second syllable' but 'the final/major syllable'.
new_statements.identity_note: Buakaw 2012 describes two varieties, both Pale/Silver Palaung [pce] = Ruching Palaung: Dara-ang of No-Lae village, Fang district, Chiang Mai (Thailand) and Da-ang of Nyaung Gone village, Kalaw, southern Shan State (Myanmar); the stress statement is made for each. Per Buakaw (p. 16), Janzen 1978's 'Pale' or 'Di-ang' is the Kalaw Da-ang variety; Kasisopa 2003 describes the No-Lae Dara-ang variety.

new_statements.quote: p.58 (§4.4): "...พยางค์รองในภาษาดาระอั้ง บ้านนอแลนี้ มักจะไม่ได้รับการลงเสียงหนัก ส่วนพยางค์หลักในคำ 2 พยางค์นั้น จะได้รับการลงเสียงหนักเสมอ"; p.93 (§6.1.1.3): "โดยพยางค์หลักจะเป็นพยางค์ที่สื่อความหมายของคำซึ่งจะได้รับการลงเสียงหนักเสมอ ขณะที่พยางค์รองซึ่งอาจเป็นพยางค์แรกของคำผสมที่กร่อนไป หรือเป็นหน่วยคำเติมหน้าศัพท์ โดยปกติจะไม่ได้รับการลงเสียงหนัก"; p.47 (§4.3): "เสียงกลางระดับ [33] ปรากฏในพยางค์รองเป็นส่วนมาก เนื่องจากพยางค์รองเป็นพยางค์ที่ไม่ได้รับการลงเสียงหนัก จึงทำให้เกิดความเป็นกลางขึ้น (neutralization)"
new_statements.translation: p.58: '...the minor syllable in Dara-ang of Ban Nawlae usually does not receive stress, whereas the major syllable in a two-syllable word always receives stress.' p.93: 'the major syllable is the syllable that carries the word's meaning and always receives stress, while the minor syllable, which may be the eroded first syllable of a compound or a prefix, normally does not receive stress.' p.47: 'mid-level pitch [33] occurs mostly in minor syllables; because the minor syllable does not receive stress, neutralization arises.' Also English abstract: 'Dara-ang is not a tonal language. However, 4 different pitches can be heard ... pitches can be taken as the phonetic characteristics of syllable structures.'

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and type as the catalog record from Buakaw 2012 (stressed major/main syllable preceded by unstressed reduced minor syllable(s) = final stress, final stress) for the same village variety (Dara-ang of No Lae / Nawlae, Fang, Chiang Mai). Adds: explicit 'always stressed' for the major syllable, pitch neutralisation to mid [33] in unstressed minor syllables, and an explicit non-tonal/non-register analysis with 4 predictable phonetic pitches.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are monosyllables, minor+major (sesquisyllabic) disyllables, compounds or longer strings; the major syllable (the meaning-bearing, final syllable of a minor+major word) always carries stress, and the preceding minor syllable (CV- with /k ʔ d m s w/ + /a ə i/, or a homorganic syllabic nasal), being a reduced first syllable or prefix, is normally unstressed; i.e. word stress is fixed on the final (major) syllable. The language is analysed as non-tonal and non-register: four phonetic pitches [33 22 44/45 232/352] are predictable from syllable type and coda, with unstressed minor syllables neutralised to mid [33].
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged wording only: minor syllables 'usually/normally' (มักจะ / โดยปกติ) unstressed; no statement on stress in compounds of two major syllables or in longer polysyllables; no exceptions listed.
new_statements.identity_note: Kasisopa 2003 describes Dara-ang (self-name; Thai ดาระอั้ง; exonym Palaung ปะหล่อง) as spoken at Ban Nawlae (No Lae), Fang district, Chiang Mai, Thailand, by speakers who migrated from the Doi Lai area, Shan State, Myanmar (3 main consultants aged 40-52, 10 speakers for acoustics) = the same village variety as Buakaw 2012's 'Dara-ang of No-Lae', classed by Glottolog under ruch1235 (Ruching/Pale Palaung). Janzen 1978 concerns Pale (Da-ang/Southern Ta-ang of the Kalaw area) compared with Gold (Shwe) and Rumai Palaung.

sources.note: No prose statement on stress. Da-ang (Kalaw) is the Pale/Silver Palaung variety (pce). Phonetic transcriptions of sesquisyllabic words consistently place primary stress on the major (final) syllable: [saˈpən] 'lips', [saˈnaʔ] 'tender', [sɔˈdaːʔ] 'hot' (ex. 1, p.6); [kaˈtɛː] 'center', [kaˈpɔː] 'gourd', [ʔaˈsei] 'who', [maˈnou] 'teach' (ex. 2-3, p.7); uses the term 'major open syllables' (p.7).
